title: Foundation Models
answer: Every released model, by modality and purpose, with full release, licence, architecture, context, pricing, performance, and safety metadata.

reading.body:
Foundation models are catalogued by purpose and modality, not by size or compute, and the largest categories are vision, at 1,500 models, and large language models, at 1,000.

The catalogue splits into nineteen categories. Ten of them sit at exactly 1,000, which reads as a cap rather than a count, so those numbers describe the ceiling of the listing and not the true population of released models. Only three categories fall below it: reasoning models at 330, scientific models at 806, and small language models at 50. That last figure is the most informative number here, because its membership rule is the strictest: a declared parameter count of four billion or fewer from safetensors metadata, with models that do not publish a count excluded. The scarcity is partly a real shortage of small models and partly a reporting artifact, since undisclosed sizes are dropped.

The categories are defined by tags and packaging rather than by capability. Coding models are the Hub's code tag on text-generation models, on-device models are the GGUF tag, and scientific, medical, legal, and financial models are tag-based slices. This matters for AI because tags and file formats are how models actually reach users, and they determine what can be counted at all. A model that runs locally in GGUF is a different deployment proposition from one that only exists behind an API, and the catalogue can see the first and not the second.

What this does not cover is compute, power, or buildings. There is no parameter total, no training cost, no accelerator count, and no data centre or grid figure anywhere in the record. The metadata standard promises release, licence, architecture, context, pricing, performance, and safety fields per model, but no values are given here. So this is a map of what exists and how it is labelled, not a measure of what it costs to run.

items.claim: Magic.dev's experimental LTM-2-mini research model claims a 100-million-token context window.
A 2026 head-to-head benchmark found long-context prompting scored higher on correctness but at 26 times the per-query token cost of RAG.
items.source_title: [2606.20898] The Token Tax of Epistemic Accuracy: Comparing RAG and Long-Context Architectures for Document-Grounded Generative AI Applications

items.claim: The FDA's Elsa AI platform pairs document search with mandatory human verification at every stage.
items.source_title: FDA Expands AI Capabilities and Completes Data Platform Consolidation

items.claim: Mistral Large 3 has 675 billion total parameters and 41 billion active parameters.
Mistral Large 3 was released in December 2025 under the Apache 2.0 license.
Mistral raised a 1.7 billion euro Series C in September 2025 at an 11.7 billion euro post-money valuation, led by ASML with a 1.3 billion euro investment.
items.source_title: Mistral AI raises 1.7B€ to accelerate technological progress with AI

items.claim: On ARC-AGI-2, a top verified commercial model scored 37.6% at $2.20 per task, while a more expensive refinement-loop configuration reached 54% at $30 per task.
